title: Molokhia
subtitle: Egyptian green herb soup with chicken and garlic
excerpt: Molokhia is a thick, vibrantly green soup made from the leaves of the jute plant, simmered in chicken stock and finished with a fierce pouring of fried garlic and coriander. It is the national comfort food of Egypt, eaten with rice and pulled chicken, and has a distinctively gelatinous, silky texture.
sourceNotes: Molokhia (also written mulukhiyah) is the national dish of Egypt and is also eaten across Lebanon, Jordan, and Tunisia. The word refers to the plant (Corchorus olitorius, or jute). Frozen molokhia leaves are sold in Middle Eastern grocery shops in the UK.

recipe.freezeNotes: The cooked soup does not freeze well; the texture changes on thawing.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The poached chicken can be prepared the day before. Make the soup fresh on the day.

content.text: Molokhia is not a dish that looks dramatic. The colour is vivid green and the texture is gelatinous; people who have not eaten it before sometimes hesitate. But one spoonful changes things. The soup has a deep, rounded, garlicky flavour and a silky body that makes it feel simultaneously light and filling.

The most important moment in making molokhia is the ta'leya: the pour. Garlic and coriander seeds are fried to the edge of burning in a separate small pan, then poured sizzling into the soup. The oil carries the scent through the whole pot immediately.
Frozen molokhia leaves are sold in Egyptian, Lebanese, and other Middle Eastern grocery shops. Use them straight from frozen; do not thaw first or they will become waterlogged.

items.prepNote: frozen leaves, straight from the freezer

content.text: Make the stock and cook the chicken

Place the chicken in a large pot with the onion, bay leaves, allspice, and salt. Cover with 1.5 litres of water. Bring to the boil, skim off any foam, then simmer for 35 minutes until the chicken is cooked through. Remove the chicken and shred the meat from the bones. Strain the stock and return 1 litre to the pot.

Bring the strained stock to a gentle boil. Add the frozen molokhia leaves straight from the freezer. Stir to break them up and simmer for 5 minutes until the leaves are completely thawed and the soup has thickened and turned deep green. Add the lemon juice.

Heat the vegetable oil in a small frying pan over high heat until very hot. Add the crushed garlic and fry for 30 seconds until golden but not burnt. Add the ground coriander, stir for 10 seconds, then pour the entire contents of the pan into the molokhia soup. It will sizzle loudly. Stir immediately. Taste and adjust the salt. Serve over white rice with the shredded chicken alongside.

rows.cause: Too much stock or leaves not fully cooked
rows.fix: Simmer for 3 to 5 more minutes. As the leaves cook fully they release their natural thickening.

rows.symptom: Garlic burnt rather than golden in the ta'leya
rows.cause: Heat too high or left too long
rows.fix: Work quickly. The garlic needs only 30 seconds over high heat. Have the soup pot nearby ready for the pour.
Add the molokhia and cook only until just thawed and bright green, not beyond. The ta'leya goes in last.

content.text: In Lebanon, molokhia is served with a tomato and onion sauce (called dagga) poured alongside rather than mixed in. In Tunisia, dried molokhia leaves are ground to a powder and cooked into a completely different, denser dish with lamb.
Poach the chicken and make the stock a day ahead. Refrigerate separately. Make the soup and ta'leya fresh on the day of serving; the green colour and garlic scent do not hold well once made.

Molokhia is the everyday soul food of Egypt. It is eaten for lunch and dinner at family tables across the country. In Cairo it is as familiar as a tomato soup might be in the UK. Its distinctive texture and colour make it instantly recognisable to anyone who has eaten it, and deeply nostalgic for Egyptians living abroad.
